analysis.one_liner: Requires internet providers to get your permission before sharing or selling your sensitive data.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from April 2017 until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Federal Communications Commission to write rules requiring internet and phone companies to tell customers what data they collect and how they use it. Companies would need your affirmative opt-in consent before using or sharing sensitive information like your web browsing history, precise location, health or financial details, or the content of your communications. It also would have barred companies from refusing service to customers who say no to data use, and required basic data security and breach notifications.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband, wireless, and phone customers. The bill would have given them a real say over data that carriers collect simply for providing service, including which websites they visit and where they are physically located. It also would have protected former customers and even people who applied for service but never bought it.

how_it_helps.text: Carriers would need opt-in consent before using or sharing sensitive customer data, including browsing history, app usage, precise geolocation, financial and health information, Social Security numbers, children's data, call records, and the content of communications.

Carriers would have to tell customers at the point of sale what information they collect, how they use and share it, and who they share it with, and notify customers of material privacy-policy changes.
Carriers could not refuse to serve customers who decline to consent to commercial use of their data, ending 'take-it-or-leave-it' offers.
Carriers would have to adopt reasonable data security practices and notify customers of security breaches, and the FCC would have to protect de-identified data from being re-identified.
The FCC would have had 180 days after enactment to issue the rules, with the rules taking effect 180 days after that.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband, wireless, and telecom carriers. They would lose a revenue stream built on analyzing and sharing customer data for targeted advertising, and would face compliance costs for notice, consent, security, and breach-notification requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill regulated only carriers, not edge providers like Google and Facebook; a carrier's rivals could keep monetizing similar behavioral data without the same consent rules, which the industry argued was one-sided regulation.

Opt-in consent for browsing and app-usage data would limit the data available for personalized offerings and advertising-supported models, a real cost the carriers would bear, and some of which could be passed to customers.
The 180-day deadline for the FCC to write comprehensive privacy regulations was aggressive for a rulemaking of this scope, raising the risk of rushed or litigation-prone rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary people is substantial and concrete: control over browsing history, location, and communications content that carriers currently collect as a byproduct of service. The main costs fall on carriers in lost ad-targeting revenue and compliance work. The strongest good-faith objection, that web companies were left unregulated while carriers were not, is an argument for broader privacy rules rather than for leaving carrier data use unrestricted. On balance the bill's benefits outweigh its costs for customers, though its narrow scope was a legitimate weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2017 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the bill on April 6, 2017, joined by 12 cosponsors (11 Democrats and 1 Independent).
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on April 6, 2017.
No further action was recorded: the committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill's timing mattered: it came weeks after Congress repealed, and the President signed into law, a resolution nullifying the FCC's 2016 broadband privacy rules, and this bill was an attempt to put similar protections back in statute.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband and wireless carriers came out ahead: because the bill died, they continue to collect and monetize customer data such as browsing history and location without a federal opt-in consent requirement. Internet advertising giants like Google and Facebook also benefit relatively, since they remain untouched by any comparable consent rules for behavioral data.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband carriers and web ad giants

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its introduction with 12 cosponsors

for.name: 11 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Blumenthal, Warren, Sanders, Merkley, Heinrich, Udall, Leahy, Baldwin, Van Hollen, and Franken

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. John Thune (R-SD)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled, so the bill never reached the Senate floor

against.name: Broadband and telecom industry
against.role: Major carriers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Fought successfully weeks earlier to repeal the FCC's 2016 broadband privacy rules through the Congressional Review Act and opposed their return in any form

against.name: 115th Congress and President Trump
against.role: Congress passed the CRA resolution nullifying the FCC's 2016 privacy rules; the President signed it in April 2017, and the FCC under its new chairman declined to reimpose them
against.what_they_did: Removed the existing broadband privacy rules just before this bill was introduced, eliminating the rules the bill sought to restore

sides.party_line_note: All 13 Senate supporters were Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would require opt-in consent before carriers use or sell sensitive customer data like browsing history and location, directly cutting into their data-driven advertising revenue. Their interest in keeping that data freely usable runs against customers' privacy interests. Because the bill died, carriers keep their current data practices unchanged.

industries.industry: Internet advertising platforms and data brokers
industries.note: The bill covered only carriers, not web giants like Google and Facebook. Its death preserves the competitive and regulatory asymmetry: behavioral advertising continues at scale, with no comparable federal opt-in consent rules for the data these companies collect.
